newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND AND GHEDINA CHASE FIRST GOLDS.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND AND GHEDINA CHASE FIRST GOLDS.

text.p: Luc Alphand and Kristian Ghedina, two men who have never won gold medals, may find Saturday's downhill at the Alpine skiing world championships brings further disappointment.
The Frenchman, dubbed "Unlucky Luc" in the past because of his injury problems, and the Italian arrived in Sestriere with high hopes but both seem to be suffering.
Alphand is nursing a bout of influenza and has been on antibiotics since Monday, while Ghedina is still sore from a fall in the Swiss resort of Wengen last month.
Ghedina slipped and crashed into an advertising hoarding after crossing the finish area in first place at that World Cup race, his third victory of the season.
Alphand also has three World Cup wins and heads the downhill standings ahead of the Italian.
The Frenchman has competed in four world championships but done no better than fourth in 1993 and third behind Austria's Patrick Ortlieb and Ghedina last year.
"I'm getting there," said the 31-year-old Alphand, winner of the World Cup downhill title for the past two seasons.
This week, neither men was much pleased with the world championship Kandahar Banchetta piste.
"The middle section is so flat you can't get any speed. It's boring and more of a super-G," Alphand said after the first of three training runs.
But while Alphand appears to have come to terms with the slope after clocking two second-fastest training times, Ghedina posted only a seventh and a ninth quickest time.
"The piste was so-so and I was also just so-so," said Ghedina, a target of autograph seekers this week in the absence of Alberto Tomba.
Tough competition will undoubtedly come from the only other triumphant downhill skier this winter, Austria's Fritz Strobl, who captured his first World Cup victories in Val D'Isere and Kitzbuehel.
Unlike Alphand and Ghedina, Strobl likes the course in Sestriere.
"This is a great slope, there are a lot of bumps and jumps. I will definitely improve my jumps here if nothing else," Strobl said after posting the best training time in the first run.
His team mate Werner Franz will also be a man to watch.
Franz is not only seeking gold on Saturday but also wants to beat Strobl, who has denied him a first World Cup win by a few fractions of a second on two occasions this winter.
"The day will come when I will beat Fritz, maybe it will be at the championships.

"Everytime I get to the finish area, a Strobl seems to be in the lead," he said after Monday's practice in reference to Fritz's namesake and compatriot Josef Strobl -- another favourite for the blue-riband event.
Ortlieb will be looking to defend his title but the big man's chances appear slim as his form has not been the best this winter due to injuries.
"I will try my best but it won't be the end of the world if I don't succeed," said Ortlieb, the Olympic champion.

Attention will also be focused on the Norwegian team, who have already clinched two golds and a silver in Sestriere, with Atle Skaardal and Lasse Kjus first and second in super-G and Kjetil Andre Aamodt taking the combined title.
Although Skaardal is the only Norwegian to have stood on a downhill World Cup podium this season with two second places, Kjus and Aamodt have a habit of coming good when it matters.

Swiss hopes of a first gold since 1993 rest with Bruno Kernen, a surprise silver medallist in Thursday's combined despite a bad fall in Wengen in January, and William Besse, who has had two podium finishes this season.
